newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Kinkel brings plan to Bosnia for refugee return.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel brings plan to Bosnia for refugee return.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel visits Sarajevo on Thursday to try to coordinate Bosnian refugee repatriation plans which have been criticised for being chaotic, inconsistent and, in some cases, inhumane.

His ministry said he would lead a delegation of leaders from Germany's 16 states, which took in about 320,000 refugees during the 1992-95 war and which last October decided to compel them to go back if they failed to return of their own accord.

It will also include Josef Vosen, mayor of the town of Dueren near the Dutch border, who has come up with an original concept of returning refugees to housing close to, if not immediately in their home towns in a way that will avoid making them a burden on Bosnian authorities.

The plan to help refugees who were "ethnically cleansed" has the backing of the German government, the European Union, the UNHCR refugee agency and refugees themselves and it could act as a model for other German officials facing such problems.
It envisages giving every returnee a lump sum of 2,500 marks ($1,440) -- a fraction of the cost of maintaining them in Germany -- and providing them with EU-funded housing.
The Bosnian government has yet to approve, but Vosen said he hoped the trip would help them decide to agree to it.
"We don't want to force them to go home. We want them to be able to go home voluntarily -- but at the same time not be a burden on the town that takes them in," Vosen told Reuters.

"The Bosnian government agreed to let them come back as part of the scheme last month but a week later said they could not agree to it because it violated Dayton by failing to settle refugees back in their home towns," Vosen said in a reference to the Dayton accords that ended the war in Bosnia.

"But if they stay here it would also mean ethnic division and that's also against Dayton. We have to decide what is Dayton and what is not. But if this scheme does not work, nothing will," Vosen said, speaking from Dueren.

With memories of World War Two still poignant, Germans welcomed the refugees with open arms taking in more than the rest of the European Union. But, facing record unemployment and economic decline at home, Germans started to complain the Bosnians were becoming a burden on increasingly tight finances.

Some states, such as Berlin and arch-conservative Bavaria, have already taken advantage of the decision by regional interior ministers last October, and chartered planes to take hundreds of refugees back under German police escort.
But many Social Democrat-ruled regions and towns, like Dueren, have balked at such measures, calling them inhumane.
Refugee agencies have sharply criticised the policy saying that many returnees had ended up in refugee camps and their return had compounded Bosnia's post-war chaos and instability.

Dueren took in about 600 refugees. Of those 220 Moslems are from the town of Modrica which now is occupied by Serbs making it impossible for them to return. Vosen proposes they settle in the nearby Moslem-controlled town of Gradacac.
Dueren would give each refugee 2,500 marks and a family of four would receive about 10,000 marks which would go a long way in Bosnia, where the average monthly income is about 200 marks.

The EU has agreed to pay 1.8 million marks for the construction of about 50 flats for them by Bosnian contractors to bring some jobs to the region. These could be portable buildings to keep open the option of eventually moving them and the community back to Modrica, Vosen said.
Dueren has ordered a pre-fabricated kindergarten and school to send there along with 17 industrial sewing machines to help set up a factory. ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
